_comment: Drafted final responses, written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) after reading each scenario's observed tool results. response_for is the observed_digest they were written against; capture marks a candidate stale_response if it changes. Pending human review.

spec-route-bone-xray.response:
Two models can run here now for bone X-ray feature extraction: rad-dino and resnet50-a1-in1k. Three more are compatible but blocked: dinov2-base, biomedclip and medsiglip-448 are still catalog-only (evidence_state cataloged, inference permission unreviewed, no adapter).

Both runnable models are frozen encoders. They return a feature vector per image, not a prediction, so classifying anything needs a head fitted and evaluated on top. Neither has been validated on bone tumors.

spec-bone-segmentation.response:
No. The catalog's only segmentation task is brain_tumor_segmentation, and routing it for bone X-rays returned no compatible model. The one segmentation model, monai-brats-mri-segmentation, is for brain MRI, not radiographs.

So nothing here can outline bone tumors today. BTXRD does ship tumor boxes and polygons, which a future segmentation model could be trained on, but no such model exists in this catalog.

spec-detector-not-probability.response:
No. It is a detector: its native output is 3D boxes labeled 'nodule' with a detection-confidence score each. That score says how confident it is that a box contains a nodule, not whether the nodule is cancer, and its record states it says nothing about malignancy.

It also can't run here yet: it is catalog-only, with no adapter and unreviewed inference permission. A malignancy estimate would need a different model, trained and evaluated against pathology-confirmed labels.

spec-encoder-vs-segmenter.response:
No, they do different jobs. RAD-DINO is a frozen encoder for X-rays: it turns one radiograph into a 768-number feature vector and makes no findings. The BraTS bundle is a 3D segmenter for brain MRI: it needs four co-registered sequences (T1c, T1, T2, FLAIR) and outputs masks for tumor core, whole tumor and enhancing tumor.

Different inputs, different outputs and different questions. RAD-DINO can run here for research use; the BraTS model is catalog-only with no adapter.

spec-risk-model.response:
We don't have one. A catalog search for 'risk' returns nothing.

A risk model outputs a calibrated probability of an outcome for a defined population. The kinds of model in this catalog don't do that: encoders give feature vectors, detectors give boxes with confidence scores and segmenters give masks, and none of those is a per-patient percentage. Building one would need patient-level data with outcomes for the population you care about.

spec-embed-ask-malignant.response:
RAD-DINO ran on btxrd:IMG000001 and returned a 768-dimensional embedding (L2 norm 15.175, vector SHA-256 ab17a800...1902). It came from model.safetensors with SHA-256 dbfb9f54...91ae at revision 110cbc18, using the default 'pad' preprocessing.

That is a feature vector, not a malignancy call. RAD-DINO has no classifier, and the result says so. To score malignant, benign or normal you would need a head fitted on BTXRD features and evaluated, and anything like that here is exploratory and image-level only. I can't tell you whether this image is malignant from this output.

spec-embed-resnet.response:
ResNet-50 returned a 2048-dimensional embedding for btxrd:IMG000002 (L2 norm 4.920, vector SHA-256 6286819a...edd4). The input file's SHA-256 is f7b58cd9...bbf.

The files behind it: model.safetensors, SHA-256 773525d5...41bb (102,469,840 bytes), and the timm processor config.json, SHA-256 ff00d936...ac50, at revision 76726860. Preprocessing was 'pad': grayscale, padded to a square, bicubic resize to 288, ImageNet mean and std.

It is a feature vector from an ImageNet backbone, not a prediction.

data-split-by-patient.response:
I can't make a patient split for BTXRD. Its record says the release has no patient or lesion ID, and the paper notes several views can show the same lesion, so I would have to guess who is who.

What I can do is an image-level 70/15/15 split that keeps the 21 exact-duplicate pairs together. Results from it are exploratory and probably optimistic, because views of one patient can land on both sides. A real patient split needs a pseudonymous patient or lesion map from the dataset maintainers.

data-infer-patients.response:
I'd rather not. Rows that share center, age and gender are not the same patient: unrelated people share those values, and one patient's views could be split apart. The audit workflow rules out inferring patients from filenames, order, age, gender or center for that reason.

A wrong grouping is worse than none, because it makes a split look patient-independent when it isn't. Keep the work image-level and labeled exploratory, and ask the maintainers for a real mapping.

data-evidence-needed.response:
Before a responsible train-and-evaluate on BTXRD, these are missing:

1. A patient or lesion mapping. The release has none, and several views can show one lesion.
2. The reference standard per row. The paper says histology or two radiology experts, but not which applies to each image.
3. Adjudication of the two byte-identical pairs labeled benign in one copy and normal in the other (IMG000591/IMG003456, IMG000707/IMG003346).
4. A human review of the near-duplicate candidates, adding confirmed same-image pairs to duplicate groups.
5. A check for overlap with other public bone X-ray sets.
6. An evaluation source nobody has examined yet, since centers 2 and 3 have already been used as test data.

Until then, results stay image-level and exploratory.

data-cbis-grouping.response:
Yes, a patient-level split is possible. CBIS-DDSM has 1,566 participants carrying 6,671 TCIA patient IDs, and the P_xxxxx participant ID groups all of a participant's IDs. That grouping was verified against the collection page.

The official split isn't safe as it stands. It was made separately for mass and calcification cases, so 31 participants appear in both a train and a test file. Regroup by participant before splitting. The per-row pathology reference standard hasn't been reviewed yet, and nothing is downloaded: the collection is 163 GB, so you would fetch a patient subset.

data-nodulemnist-labels.response:
No. NoduleMNIST3D's benign and malignant labels come from radiologist malignancy suspicion ratings in LIDC-IDRI, not confirmed diagnosis.

Two more cautions: the release has no patient IDs, so several nodules can come from one patient across splits, and its source overlaps the MONAI lung detector's training data.

data-lidc-eval-detector.response:
Not as an accuracy measurement. The MONAI detector was trained on LUNA16, which is derived from LIDC-IDRI, so our sample is not independent of its training data. The sample is also only 3 patients and 3 CT series, without the radiologist annotation files, so there is no reference to score against.

On top of that, the detector is catalog-only here, with no adapter. The sample is useful for DICOM ingestion and an adapter smoke test, not evaluation.

data-duplicates.response:
Yes. BTXRD has 21 byte-identical image pairs; splits keep each pair together. Two of those pairs carry conflicting labels (benign in one copy, normal in the other), so all four images are left unlabeled.

A feature-similarity search also found further near duplicates and likely same-patient pairs, many of which cross an image-stratified split. Those are candidates for human review, not confirmed groups yet.

data-breastmnist-units.response:
The number of patients is unknown. BreastMNIST has 780 grayscale ultrasound images at 28 x 28 (a 224 x 224 version too): 546 train, 78 validation, 156 test.

Labels are binary. Local counts for index 0 and 1 are 147/399 in train, 21/57 in validation and 42/114 in test. MedMNIST documents 0 as malignant and 1 as normal or benign; that wasn't re-checked against the source here. The splits may not respect source patients, so use it for pipeline tests, not performance claims.

train-plan-rad-dino.response:
A plan that fits what's here:

1. Fix the endpoint and label order first. BTXRD supports three-class, tumor vs normal and benign vs malignant, and none is decided yet.
2. Preprocessing: RAD-DINO takes 518 x 518 with its own mean and std. The default 'pad' keeps the whole radiograph. Pick any variant on validation data only.
3. Split: there are no patient IDs, so split by image with duplicate groups kept together and label the run exploratory. Hold a whole source out if you want a shift estimate.
4. Imbalance: report per-class recall, balanced accuracy and AP for the rare class; heads use class weights.
5. Features are bound to measured image hashes and model identity, so changed inputs or old caches are refused.
6. Budget: RAD-DINO runs about 2.3 images/s on the laptop, so all of BTXRD takes roughly half an hour.

Command: python -m cancer_workbench baseline --encoder rad-dino --endpoint three_class --protocol image_stratified

RAD-DINO is cleared for research-use inference only; sharing derived heads is unreviewed.

train-imbalance.response:
BTXRD has 1,879 normal, 1,525 benign and 342 malignant images, so malignant is about 9%.

For training, keep every image and weight classes: the heads here use balanced class weights. For metrics, overall accuracy hides the rare class, so report per-class recall, balanced accuracy and average precision for malignant, with intervals. Expect wide intervals for malignant. Those intervals resample images, so they are too narrow if images share patients, which BTXRD can't rule out.

train-interrupted.response:
Not entirely. Each encoder's feature cache is written to a temporary file and only renamed into place when it's complete, and a cache is reused when its inputs and model identity match. So encoders that already finished aren't recomputed.

The encoder that was cut off has no cache and starts over; there's no partial resume within one encoder. Rerun the same command.

train-budget.response:
From the measured rates on the 8 GB laptop: RAD-DINO runs about 2.3 images/s, so BTXRD's 3,746 images take roughly 27 minutes. ResNet-50 runs about 30-40 images/s, so about 2 minutes.

Storage is no problem. By arithmetic (images x dimension x 4 bytes) the caches are about 11.5 MB for RAD-DINO's 768 dimensions and 31 MB for ResNet-50's 2,048, next to the 840 MB BTXRD archive, well inside the 40 GB budget.

train-finetune-rad-dino.response:
Not yet. RAD-DINO's terms review allows research-use inference only; adaptation is unreviewed. MIT permits modification, but how the model card's research-only statement applies to fine-tunes is a team decision.

The reuse workflow also puts limited adaptation after a frozen baseline exists and the adaptation entry is allowed with evidence. Fine-tuning on BTXRD as it stands would also make leakage worse: there are no patient IDs and only 342 malignant images. Start with the frozen-encoder head.

train-preprocessing.response:
Not by default. ResNet-50's own test transform resizes the shortest edge to 288 and center-crops to a square. On a radiograph that can cut off a lesion near the edge. The workbench's default 'pad' keeps the whole image, padding to a square before resizing.

If you want the publisher's crop, the 'native_crop' variant matches timm exactly. Choose between them on validation data only, never on test results.

fail-empty-search.response: The catalog search for 'osteosarcoma' returned nothing, so there's no such model here to offer. If it helps, I can search for general pathology encoders instead; I won't name one without looking it up.

fail-dataset-as-model.response: That didn't run: 'btxrd' is a dataset, not a model, so run_specialist found no model with that id. To get features for IMG000001, pick an encoder with route_models and run it on btxrd:IMG000001.

fail-gated-medsiglip.response: MedSigLIP didn't run. The call was rejected because its record is still cataloged, its inference permission is unreviewed and it has no adapter. Someone has to acquire it, review its terms and install an adapter before it can embed anything.

fail-wrong-modality.response: Rejected: RAD-DINO only accepts X-rays, and the request said MRI. Also, btxrd:IMG000001 is a BTXRD bone radiograph, not a brain MRI. Which image did you mean?

fail-missing-image.response: Nothing ran: IMG999999 isn't in the BTXRD manifest. Please check the id.

fail-path-outside.response: Rejected: the encoders don't read arbitrary file paths. Inputs must be btxrd:<sample_id> or uploads:<id>. Upload the image on the Images screen and I'll run it as uploads:<id>.

fail-bad-arguments.response:
My first call was malformed: inputs must be an object, not a string. I retried with {"image": "btxrd:IMG000001"}.

ResNet-50 returned a 2048-dimensional embedding (L2 norm 5.417, vector SHA-256 24ef4261...c337) for the file with SHA-256 2ddae86a...37ad. It is a feature vector, not a prediction.

fail-catalog-only-segmenter.response: The BraTS model can't run here. The call was rejected because it is catalog-only: evidence cataloged, inference permission unreviewed, no adapter. The upload was never checked, because eligibility failed first.

fail-unknown-workflow.response: There's no workflow for federated training. The available ones cover choosing a specialist type, auditing a dataset before training, planning a frozen-encoder baseline, handling unavailable or rejected results, reading research claims and choosing a reuse path. None of them covers federated training.

research-rad-dino-clinical.response:
No. The MIT license covers copying and modifying the files, but the model card says RAD-DINO is 'shared for research purposes only' and 'not meant to be used for clinical practice'. Our terms review allows research-use inference only.

Clinical use would also need validated performance on the target population and regulatory review. Nothing here has that, and RAD-DINO only produces feature vectors.

research-btxrd-reproduced.response: No. BTXRD's record is at evidence_state cataloged, which means nothing from the paper has been reproduced here. What this repository has is different: exploratory, image-level frozen-encoder runs, not the paper's YOLOv8 setup. The paper's figures aren't in our record, so I won't quote them as if they were checked.

research-medsiglip-better.response:
There's no evidence here either way. MedSigLIP isn't acquired: its record is cataloged, with unreviewed HAI-DEF terms and no adapter, so it has never been run. RAD-DINO runs here, but its pretraining was chest X-rays only, and nothing has shown how either transfers to bone tumors.

Answering this needs both run under one matched protocol on the same images and splits, plus a check of MedSigLIP's pretraining overlap with BTXRD's sources.

research-btxrd-license.response:
BTXRD is CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), so give attribution, link the license and note any changes you make.

Cite the paper, Yao et al., Scientific Data (2025), doi:10.1038/s41597-024-04311-y, and the data release, doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.27865398.v1. A resolving DOI only identifies the source; check that the passage you cite actually supports your claim.

reuse-distill.response:
Not now. Distillation is unreviewed in RAD-DINO's terms review, and the reuse workflow needs an evaluated teacher and an allowed distillation entry first.

RAD-DINO isn't a bone-tumor teacher anyway: it is a frozen encoder with no evaluated bone outputs. A teacher would be a model evaluated on this task, and its outputs would be a separate data product with their own rights.

reuse-breast-ultrasound.response:
resnet50-a1-in1k is the only encoder that can run for breast ultrasound here. dinov2-base and biomedclip are compatible but catalog-only, and rad-dino was rejected because it only takes X-rays.

For data, BreastMNIST has 780 small ultrasound images with unknown patient grouping, so it suits pipeline tests rather than performance claims. Any head you fit is exploratory.

reuse-mammography.response:
None in the catalog. Routing feature extraction for breast mammography rejected every model: no encoder lists mammography as a modality, including ResNet-50 and RAD-DINO.

Using one anyway would mean deciding to treat mammograms as generic X-rays and recording that in the catalog, which is a review decision, not something to do silently.
